newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Petrol crunch grounds oil-producing Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Petrol crunch grounds oil-producing Nigeria.

text.p: Several parts of oil-producing Nigeria were at a near standstill on Monday from a two-week-old petrol shortage.
In Lagos, many people in Nigeria's biggest city and commercial hub, stayed home or were stranded at bus stops.
"Most of my staff have not come to work and I guess that this is because of the fuel situation," said Tokunbo Martins at his travel agency in central Lagos.
Long queues formed at the few stations still selling fuel in Lagos and motorists said after hours of waiting they had to pay far above the normal price.
"Petrol attendants prefer to sell to touts who turn round and sell to people at inflated prices," said civil servant Chuks Okoli, on a queue along Awolowo Road in Ikoyi area of Lagos.
A 50-litre (10 gallon) can of petrol was selling for 4,000 naira ($47) instead of the normal price of 550 naira ($6.47).
"This is a great shame for our oil-producing nation," commented an exasperated taxi driver.
Newspaper reports said several other cities, including the inland capital Abuja, had been hit. They said travellers faced long waits for intercity buses, while fares had doubled.
Fuel shortages occur frequently in Nigeria and usually last a few days but the current crisis shows no sign of easing.
There has been no definitive explanation of the cause from state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) nor its subsidiary the Pipelines and Products Marketing Company.
Industry sources blame the crisis on the four refineries able to process 445,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil but which operate well below that.
"The present problem lies with the supplier. Marketers are not getting enough from NNPC," said an official of one of the main petroleum products marketing firms in Nigeria.
NNPC denies there is a problem with refineries, insisting the shortage would soon end.

Newspapers on Monday quoted the chief executive of the Warri refinery in the midwest, Ezenwa Dennar, as saying the shortage was due to a crisis in Warri, where communal trouble had led to a dusk-to-dawn curfew that was impeding the delivery of fuel.
"We are not getting vessels coming to the jetty. There is a curfew in Warri and this affects distribution," Dennar said.
Nigeria, Africa's leading crude oil producer and a major player in the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries pumps around two million bpd of crude oil.
